title: London System for White
description: A simple, solid setup for White. Learn the London System moves, why the bishop comes out before e3, how to meet Black's common replies, and two easy plans.

chapters.title: Plans and when to play it

moves.comment: The pawn takes space in the center.
The knight comes out and guards d4 and e5.
This is the London System. The bishop is out, and it is outside the pawn chain.

steps.intro: The idea: build a simple, solid setup with the same few moves every game. The star is the bishop on f4.

moves.comment: The bishop steps out to f4, where it has lots of room.

hints: Use the bishop that starts on c1.
Move the bishop from c1 to f4.
steps.intro: White to move. Bring out the London bishop.

hints: Start with the queen's pawn.
Then the knight to f3.
Last, the bishop from c1 comes out.
steps.intro: Play the first three moves of the London System as White.

points: The idea in one line: build a simple, solid setup that you can use against many replies
Name the pieces as you go: pawn d4, knight f3, bishop f4
You learn one plan well instead of many lines badly
People say the name comes from a chess event held in London long ago.
mistakes: Thinking you can play the same moves with your eyes closed: always check what Black just did
Moving the same piece twice
Forgetting that Black also makes threats
questions: Which pieces have we moved after three moves?
Why is a simple setup helpful for a beginner?
Where does the bishop on f4 point?

moves.comment: The pawn on e3 shuts the diagonal.

steps.intro: Look what happens if White plays e3 too soon. The pawn blocks the bishop on c1. The bishop can only step to d2.

moves.comment: Bishop first.
Now the pawn shuts the door behind the bishop and guards it.

steps.intro: Now the right order. First the bishop goes out. Then the pawn goes to e3 and guards the bishop.

moves.comment: Bishop first. The e-pawn can move next.

hints: Use the bishop that starts on c1.
Move it to f4, before you play e3.
steps.intro: White to move. Get the bishop out before the e-pawn moves.
Think about the bishop on c1.
steps.question: Which order is better for the London System?
choices: Pawn to e3, then bishop to f4
Bishop to f4, then pawn to e3
steps.explanation: After e3 the c1 bishop cannot reach f4. So the bishop goes first.

points: A pawn on e3 closes the diagonal for the c1 bishop
Bishop first, then the pawn: the bishop gets out before the door shuts
Walk a student up to the board and show the locked bishop with their arm
This idea works for the c8 bishop too
mistakes: Playing e3 on move two and trapping the bishop behind it
Playing the bishop out and then forgetting the e3 pawn
Leaving the bishop on f4 unprotected
questions: What does the pawn on e3 do to the bishop on c1?
Why do we play e3 after the bishop is out?
Which pawn will protect the bishop on f4 later?

moves.comment: The bishop comes out on move two.
The knight follows. Now it is the same setup as before.

steps.intro: You can also bring the bishop out right away. The pieces are the same, only the order changes.

moves.comment: The bishop is out on move two.

hints: Use the bishop that starts on c1.
Move the bishop from c1 to f4.
steps.intro: White to move. Play the London bishop right now.

points: Some players put the bishop out on move two, before the knight
This is the same plan with a different move order
The opening has its own name in the index: Accelerated London System
The knight on f3 can still come next
mistakes: Forgetting that Black may reply differently, for example with a pawn to c5
Not developing the knight after the bishop is out
questions: What is different about this move order?
Which piece should come out next?
Why can the bishop come out so early?

moves.comment: The pawn guards d4 and the bishop.
This knight guards the center and leaves c3 free for a pawn.
The pawn on c3 gives d4 a second guard.

steps.intro: Here is the London setup. Pawns on d4, e3 and c3 make a solid wall. The knights are on f3 and d2. The bishop is on f4.

moves.comment: Now d4 is guarded by the pawns on c3 and e3.

hints: Use a pawn.
Move the pawn from c2 to c3.
steps.intro: White to move. Give the d4 pawn more help with a pawn move.

hints: Pawn, knight, bishop to start.
Then the e-pawn, then the second knight.
Finish with the c-pawn.
steps.intro: Play the whole setup as White.

points: Count the setup pieces: pawns d4, e3, c3, knights f3 and d2, bishops f4 and d3
The pawns on c3 and e3 guard d4
Every piece has a job: say it out loud
Black's replies may change the order, but the pieces stay the same
mistakes: Playing c3 and e3 and forgetting to develop the knights
Putting the b1 knight on c3, which blocks the c-pawn
Moving the queen out early
questions: Which pawns guard the pawn on d4?
Why does the knight go to d2 and not c3?
Which pieces are still at home?

moves.comment: The bishop looks along the diagonal toward h7.
White castles. The king is safe and the rook comes in.

steps.intro: Two more jobs: bring the light bishop to d3 and castle.

moves.comment: The bishop aims along the diagonal at h7.

hints: Use your light-squared bishop on f1.
Move the bishop from f1 to d3.
steps.intro: White to move. Bring out the last bishop to d3, aiming at h7.

moves.comment: Castled. The king is tucked away.

hints: Use your king.
Castle on the kingside: the king goes to g1.
steps.intro: White to move. Make your king safe.

points: The bishop on d3 points at the black kingside
Castling puts the king behind pawns and wakes up the rook
Do both before you start any attack
Keep the setup calm: do not rush
mistakes: Forgetting to castle
Moving the king one square at a time instead of castling.
Putting the bishop on e2 is fine, but on d3 it aims at h7.
questions: Why do we castle before attacking?
Which diagonal does the bishop on d3 use?
Which rook comes to the center after castling?

moves.comment: A small move. It makes room for the bishop.
The knight attacks the bishop.
The bishop is safe, and it still looks along the h2-b8 diagonal.

steps.intro: Black's knight can jump to h5 and attack the bishop. A pawn on h3 gives the bishop a safe home on h2.

moves.comment: Safe, and it keeps the h2-b8 diagonal.

hints: Your bishop on f4 is attacked. Move it.
Retreat the bishop to h2.
steps.intro: White to move. Your bishop is attacked by the knight on h5. Put the bishop on h2.

points: h3 is a quiet move with a job: it gives the bishop the h2 square
Black's knight can jump to h5 and attack the bishop
Pawn moves have a price: only play h3 when it has a reason
Without h3, Bg3 lets the knight take the bishop. That is why h3 first is the tidy way.
mistakes: Retreating the bishop to a square where it is still attacked
Playing h3 on move two just because
Giving the bishop up for nothing
questions: Which black piece attacks the bishop on f4?
Where can the bishop go to be safe?
What square does h3 give the bishop?

moves.comment: The black pawn hits d4.
The e-pawn guards d4.
The second knight comes out. Next comes c3.

steps.intro: Black plays ...c5 to attack the d4 pawn. White keeps calm and adds guards: e3, the knight and c3.

moves.comment: The pawn guards d4 and the bishop on f4.

hints: Use a pawn.
Move the pawn from e2 to e3.
steps.intro: White to move. The black pawn attacks d4. Guard d4 and the bishop with a pawn move.

points: The pawn on c5 attacks d4
Guard d4 with e3, Nf3 and later c3
Do not panic: we do not have to take on c5
The knight on d2 is better than the one on c3 here
mistakes: Taking on c5 without a reason
Forgetting to protect d4
Moving the bishop away and leaving d4 weak
questions: Which black pawn attacks d4?
Which of our pieces guard d4?
Which pawn move adds one more guard?

moves.comment: Black copies the bishop move.
The same move as always.
If Black trades bishops, White simply recaptures.
White can take back with the c-pawn or the queen; both are fine.

steps.intro: Black may bring the other bishop out too. That is fine. White keeps building: e3, then Bd3.

moves.comment: The bishop comes out.

hints: Use your light-squared bishop.
Move the bishop from f1 to d3.
steps.intro: White to move. Develop the bishop and face Black's bishop.

moves.comment: An even trade. Black will take back.

hints: Use your bishop on f4.
Capture the black bishop on d6.
steps.intro: White to move. Black's bishop on d6 attacks your bishop. Trade bishops by taking it.

points: If Black copies you with ...Bf5, just keep developing
A bishop trade on d3 is fine: recapture and keep going
If Black's bishop goes to d6 it attacks our bishop: trading is fine, so is retreating to g3
Do not worry about copying moves
mistakes: Rushing an attack because the bishops face each other
Forgetting to recapture after a trade
Letting the queen go out early
questions: What happens if both bishops are traded on d3?
Which two pieces can take back on d3?
Why can we trade bishops without worry?

moves.comment: Now b2 is attacked and nothing guards it.
The queen steps back and guards b2. If the black queen takes on b2, White takes the queen.

steps.intro: When the bishop leaves c1, the b2 pawn loses its guard. Black's queen on b6 attacks it.

moves.comment: Now ...Qxb2 would lose the queen to Qxb2.

hints: Use your queen.
Move the queen from d1 to c1.
steps.intro: White to move. The black queen attacks b2. Guard b2 with your queen.
Think about which piece used to guard b2.
steps.question: Why was the b2 pawn left unguarded when Black's queen went to b6?
choices: The bishop left c1 so nothing guards b2
The knight on f3 left b2
The pawn on b2 is too small
steps.explanation: The c1 bishop used to guard b2. When it went to f4, the pawn lost its guard.

points: When the c1 bishop leaves, the b2 pawn has no guard
A black queen on b6 attacks b2
One safe fix is queen to c1. Another named line is 5.Nc3, the Poisoned Pawn Variation; this lesson shows one safe fix
Always ask: what did Black's last move attack?
mistakes: Not seeing the queen attack on b2
Forgetting that b2 lost its guard when the bishop moved
Ignoring the threat and hoping Black does not see it
questions: Why is b2 not guarded after Bf4?
Which black piece attacks b2?
How can we guard b2 with the queen?

chapterList.title: Plans and when to play it

moves.comment: The pawn steps forward. The bishop and the knight on d2 both guard e4.
A knight recaptures.
The pieces are active and the lines are open.

steps.intro: When the setup is ready, White can push the e-pawn. It challenges Black's d5 pawn and opens lines for the pieces.

moves.comment: The pawn challenges d5.

hints: Use a pawn.
Move the pawn from e3 to e4.
steps.intro: White to move. Push the e-pawn break: e3 to e4.

hints: Start with the queen's pawn, then the knight, then the bishop.
After e3, bring the other knight and the other bishop.
Push the pawn on e3 to e4 when everything is ready.
steps.intro: Play the setup and the e4 break as White.

points: A pawn break means pushing a pawn to challenge the enemy pawns
Push e4 only when your pieces are ready to recapture
After the pawn trade, lines open for the bishops and knights
This is a plan, not a rule: sometimes it is better to wait
mistakes: Pushing e4 before the knights and bishop are developed
Pushing e4 when it only loses the pawn
questions: Which of our pieces guard the e4 square?
What happens to the lines when pawns are traded?

lessons.title: Plan two: the knight to e5

moves.comment: The knight lands on a strong square.
Black attacks the knight, but it is still safe. It is guarded twice, by the d4 pawn and the bishop on f4.

steps.intro: The knight on f3 can jump to e5. The d4 pawn and the bishop on f4 both guard it, so it is safe.

moves.comment: The knight is guarded twice, by d4 and by the bishop on f4.

hints: Use the knight on f3.
Jump the knight from f3 to e5.
steps.intro: White to move. The e5 square is safe and strong. Put the knight there.

points: e5 is a strong square for the knight: the d4 pawn and the f4 bishop both guard it
From e5 the knight points at f7, d7 and c6
Black can trade it off, and that is okay
Check that the knight cannot be taken for free before you jump
mistakes: Jumping to e5 when a black piece can capture it for free
Forgetting to guard the knight
Moving the knight again and again with no plan
questions: Which of our pieces guard e5?
Can any black piece take the knight on e5 right now?
What squares does the knight attack from e5?

steps.intro: Play the London when you want a calm, solid game with a clear setup. Still check every Black move for threats. Your plans: push e4, or send the knight to e5.
Think about the London bishop.
steps.question: You play 1.d4 and Black replies 1...d5. Which is a London System move?
steps.explanation: 2.Bf4 brings out the London bishop before e3.

hints: Pawn, knight, bishop.
Then e3, the other knight, the other bishop.
Then c3 and castle.
steps.intro: Play the whole London setup, castling at the end.

points: Good for players who want a plan they can remember
It is solid and quiet, so you must still look for tactics
Not a magic trick: other openings are fine too
Ask the student how they feel about quiet positions
mistakes: Playing the moves from memory without looking at Black's last move
Never castling
Avoiding all trades and all plans
questions: Why might a beginner like a simple setup?
What do we check before every move?
What are your two plans after the setup?
